description:
We are tackling the "Interplanetary Survival Guide: Martian Map" challenge in Sapporo! Goal: build a spatial data & routing tool for Martian explorers.

I'm Joji Onuki, a full-stack dev student at Nihon University.
summary:
Martian Map is a mission-control web app for planning “Mars walks,” the on-foot moonwalk-style excursions (EVAs) future astronauts will make at Jezero Crater. It combines four NASA and USGS sources into one layered map: MRO CTX imagery, terrain models from CTX and MGS MOLA, USGS geologic maps, and the traverse records of the Mars 2020 Perseverance rover.

The app scores walking risk for every 40-meter cell using slope and surface roughness. It then uses A* search, a standard shortest-path method, to find the safest route between two points. Next, it checks the whole excursion against real Martian daylight, calculated with NASA’s Mars24 method, and a 7-hour life-support budget. The result is a clear GO, CAUTION or NO-GO decision with its reasons. Finally, astronauts can rehearse the walk in a simulation, with shadows that move with the Sun and live readouts of elapsed time, time left before sunset and life-support budget used.

Mars data today is spread across missions and archives, and none of it answers the two questions that matter most on foot: where is it dangerous, and when must we turn back? Martian Map turns decades of robotic exploration into practical decisions for the first humans on Mars. It does all its calculations with Mars’s own radius and clock, and it runs entirely in the browser with no server.
details:
What it does. Martian Map is a mission-control web app for planning "Mars walks": EVAs on foot that future astronauts will make at Jezero Crater. It answers the two questions that matter most to someone walking on Mars: where is it dangerous, and when must we turn back?

How it works. The app fuses four NASA and USGS data sources into one layered map: the Mars 2020 TRN CTX terrain model (MRO CTX and MGS MOLA), the CTX orthoimage mosaic, the USGS geologic map of Jezero Crater (SIM 3464), and Perseverance's traverse and raw images. Eight layers can be toggled, and a terrain probe shows elevation, slope, risk and geologic unit anywhere on the map. A Python pipeline turns the terrain into a 40 m grid and rates every cell as safe, caution (slope of 15° or more, or relief of 6 m or more) or no-go (slope of 30° or more, or no data). An A* search running in a Web Worker finds the lowest-risk route, with Direct, Balanced and Safest presets. The whole EVA is then checked against real Martian daylight, computed with NASA GISS's Mars24 algorithm, and a 7-hour life-support budget, giving a GO, CAUTION or NO-GO verdict with its reasons. For example, departing at 16:30 is NO-GO because the crew would return after sunset. Finally, crews can rehearse the walk in a simulation with live timers and shadows that move with the Sun, and export the route as GeoJSON.

Benefits and impact. Mars data is scattered across missions and archives, and none of it directly answers a walker's questions. Martian Map turns decades of robotic exploration into practical decisions for the first humans on Mars, and gives students and the public an intuitive way to explore Jezero Crater.

Tools and technology. Next.js, TypeScript, MapLibre GL JS, Zustand, Tailwind CSS and Vitest for the web app; Python with rasterio, numpy and geopandas for the data pipeline. It is a static site with no server and no API key. The live app (https://joji-onuki.github.io/martian-map/) runs on the real USGS terrain and imagery for western Jezero Crater.

Creativity and considerations. Web-map libraries assume Earth and would overstate distances on Mars by about 1.9 times, so every distance uses the Mars radius (3,389.5 km), and the 3D terrain is scaled by about 1.88 to restore true relief. Mars time matches NASA's published Mars24 examples in automated tests. Walking speed follows Tobler's hiking function (3 km/h on flat ground), with outbound and return legs timed separately. Known limits: risk uses slope and relief only (no rock density yet), weather is not live, and the area covers western Jezero only. Next steps are HiRISE 1 m terrain, MEDA weather records from PDS, and other landing sites, since the pipeline is site-independent.

AI use. Claude Code (Anthropic) was used to help write the code, tests and documentation, and Claude helped draft the demo deck; the one AI-generated illustration in the deck carries a visible watermark, and the other images are app screenshots.
